Student Works

Turning a franchise's paper-and-spreadsheet operations into one connected platform.

Role
Solo Product Designer
Core responsibility
UX & UI Design
Design System
Business Logic & Flows
AI-assisted Prototyping
Team
Client stakeholders
Product Manager
Business Analyst
Developers
Timeline
2 years
3 scopes

Brief

Student Works is a Canadian home-services franchise where students run their own regional businesses. Its platform covers the whole operation: hiring and training teams, selling jobs, tracking field work and paying everyone.

The legacy system left information scattered across paper notes, spreadsheets and disconnected tools. Field work was re-typed back at the office, each team kept its own copy of the data, and the franchise was getting harder to scale.

I was the only product designer on the new platform, from the first wireframe through three scopes and two years.

Project snapshot.

What changed

  • Five connected modules, from workforce to compensation.
  • No paper forms left to re-enter at the office.
  • Accounting moved onto the new platform without having to relearn their work.

Two years, three scopes.

The platform grew in stages. Each scope built on the one before it, so every decision had to hold up for what came next.

  1. Core operations

    Hiring, training, sales and field work

    Designed the connected flow for running a franchise: hiring and training teams, selling jobs and recording work in the field.

  2. Accounting & payroll

    Bringing Accounting onto the platform

    Connected payroll and compensation to everything before it, while keeping Accounting's familiar tables, terms and shortcuts.

  3. Enhancement

    Refining what was live

    Improved existing flows based on how people actually used them, with AI-assisted prototypes making each review round faster.

Where things broke down.

I learned the problems from two sources: ongoing feedback from the client, and watching how each team actually worked with the old system.

Before: estimates were knocked on doors and written by hand, then re-typed at the office.

Information lived in pieces

Field work was written on paper, then typed back in at the office. People, training, sales, field work and pay sat in separate places, so the same data was entered again and again.

Two audiences, opposite needs

Operators and admins wanted a faster, modern way of working. Accounting relied on habits built over years and wanted nothing to move.

Strict rules, many hand-offs

Payroll, permissions and notifications followed tight business rules, and the work passed between different roles. One unclear step could mean someone got paid wrong.

How might we…

  1. …capture data once and let it flow through the whole operation?Solution 1
  2. …modernize the platform without forcing Accounting to relearn their job?Solution 2
  3. …make strict rules and role hand-offs feel clear instead of risky?Solution 3

From paper notes to one connected flow.

Instead of designing five separate tools, I designed around the order the business actually runs in: hire people, train them, sell jobs, do the work, pay everyone. Each module hands its data to the next, so information is entered once, at the source.

Before

  • Hours and job details written on paper in the field
  • Re-typed into the system back at the office
  • Each team kept its own copy of the data
  • Admins chased people to know what was happening

After

  • Work is recorded once, where it happens
  • The same record moves from field work to payroll
  • Every role sees one shared version of the truth
  • Status is visible without asking anyone

One platform, two ways of changing.

Treating every user the same would have failed one group. Operators and admins were students, open to new patterns, so they got a full redesign. Accounting's speed came from years of habit, so I protected that habit and changed what happened underneath.

Operators & Admins: redesigned

  • New dashboards built around their daily tasks
  • Modern components from the shared design system
  • Status and next steps visible at a glance

Accounting: familiar on the surface

  • Kept the table layout they already scan
  • Kept their terminology, word for word
  • Kept the order of steps they follow
  • Kept keyboard shortcuts and fast data entry
  • Changed underneath: data now arrives already connected, with nothing to re-type

The trade-off was deliberate: the product carries two interaction styles. I chose adoption over strict visual consistency, and built the design system to support both modern components and dense, legacy-style tables.

Strict rules, made clear.

Much of the platform runs on rules that can't bend: who can do what, when, and in which order. Before drawing screens, I mapped each rule and its edge cases, then designed the interface so the rule is visible to the person it affects.

Payroll is prepared by one role and posted by another

Operators and admins create and review payroll for their teams, but posting it in batches belongs to Accounting. The risk lived in the hand-off: edits made after Accounting had started could break a batch.

I designed payroll as a shared record with clear stages. Each stage shows who owns it, only the owner sees the actions for that stage, and once payroll is handed over it locks for the previous role.

Notifications that leave the platform

Students in the field aren't watching a dashboard, so key moments reach them by Email and SMS through third-party services. I defined which events trigger a message, who receives it, and what each message must say so it makes sense outside the app.

Because these messages are sent by external services, I also designed what the platform shows when a message fails, so a missed notification never silently blocks someone's work.

Adapting through the shift to AI.

The project started before AI design tools were part of my work and ran straight through their rise. By the later scopes, AI wasn't a side tool any more. It changed how the whole team moved from an idea to working software.

Core operations: before AI tools

  • Static designs and prototypes built in Figma
  • Clients reviewed pictures of the product
  • Developers rebuilt every screen from a handoff file
  • Feedback rounds took days, not hours

Accounting & Enhancement: AI-assisted

  • Clickable prototypes generated with Claude and Codex
  • Clients reviewed working flows with real-looking data
  • Approved prototypes handed to devs as structured JSON
  • Business rules still checked by people, not the AI

How the team worked with AI

  1. BA & me Shape the rules

    The BA writes the user story; I add the business rules, edge cases and acceptance criteria the screen has to respect.

    User story + rules
  2. Me, with Claude Vibe the prototype

    Claude turns the story and our shared DESIGN.md into a clickable HTML prototype in hours, already using our components, colours and spacing.

    Clickable prototype
  3. Me, with Codex Harden the details

    Codex fixes states, validation and responsive edge cases, so the prototype behaves like the product rather than a picture of it.

    Working flow
  4. Client & PM Present and decide

    We walk the client through the real flow. Changes are made live during the call, so decisions happen in one meeting.

    Approved flow
  5. Me → Developers Export to JSON

    The approved prototype is exported as JSON: screens, components, fields, states and rules. Developers build from structure, not from screenshots.

    Spec developers can parse

What stayed human

  • Business rules. Every payroll and permission rule was checked against the spec by me and the BA. AI drafts; people sign off.
  • One source of style. A shared DESIGN.md kept every AI-generated screen on the same components, so speed never cost consistency.
  • Real decisions. AI produced options quickly. Choosing between them, and explaining why to the client, stayed my job.
ToolsClaudeCodexFigmaDESIGN.md

The final product.

What two years taught me.

Read expectations, not just requests

What each group asked for wasn't always what they expected. Accounting asked for features; what they really expected was not to lose their speed.

Design is coordination

Working alone on design meant constantly aligning the client, the BA and the developers. Clear rules and shared prototypes did more than any single screen.

Design for the next module

Every decision had to survive the modules that came after it. Thinking about scale early kept five modules feeling like one product.

Ecomdy

Reading the data to make a live ad platform easier to trust.

Role
Product Designer & BA, solo
Core responsibility
Tracking plan, behaviour research, UX & UI enhancement
Team
Product owner, developers
Tools
Google Analytics, Hotjar
Timeline
About 1.5 years, after launch

Context

Ecomdy helps advertisers run TikTok Ads at scale. Users get ad accounts, top up their balance, move funds between accounts, withdraw what they don't spend, and keep an eye on how their ads are spending.

My role

The product was already live when I joined. Nothing was broken, but money flows produced a steady stream of support questions and nobody could say where users dropped off. My job was to make it better without disrupting the people already using it, solo as both designer and BA.

Improve, measure, repeat.

  1. TrackDefine events that answer real questions
  2. ObserveFunnels in Google Analytics, heatmaps and recordings in Hotjar
  3. PrioritiseWeigh impact on money, reach and effort
  4. ShipSmall releases, existing paths kept
  5. MeasureSame events, before and after

First, fix the data.

The existing tracking counted page views, not what people did with their money. Before redesigning anything, I wrote a tracking plan where every event answers a question the team needed answered.

  1. topup_startedThe top-up flow opens

    How many people intend to add funds?

  2. payment_method_selectedA payment method is chosen

    Which methods do people pick, and which do they abandon?

  3. topup_submittedPayment is confirmed

    Where between intent and payment do people drop off?

  4. topup_creditedFunds reach the balance

    How long does money take to arrive?

  5. withdrawal_requestedA withdrawal is submitted

    How often do people pull money out?

  6. low_balance_shownA low-balance warning appears

    Do warnings lead to a top-up in time?

People stopped at the fee.

Signal
The biggest drop came right after a payment method was chosen. Session recordings showed people switching methods back and forth.
Insight
People weren't unsure about paying. They were unsure what they would actually receive after fees.
Change
Every method now shows its fee, processing time and the exact amount that lands in the balance, with a suggested method for the amount entered.

Waiting felt like losing money.

Signal
The largest group of tickets asked some version of "where is my money?", even though transactions were processing normally.
Insight
The interface showed nothing between submitted and done, and silence around money reads as risk.
Change
Top-ups and withdrawals became a status timeline with an expected time for each step, a notification on success or failure, and a transaction ID to share with support.

Spend lived somewhere else.

Signal
Clicks clustered on "Add Balance", "Create your Ad Account" and the support chat. The spend stats and the ad account table were almost never touched.
Insight
The overview didn't answer the question people actually had: will my ads keep running? So they checked spend in TikTok Ads Manager, or asked support, and often noticed an empty balance only after their ads had stopped.
Change
Balance, daily spend and days remaining now sit together for each account, with a low-balance warning and a one-click top-up.

Deciding what to fix first.

With one designer and a live product, the order mattered as much as the ideas. Problems that touched money and needed little effort went first, because mistakes there cost users real money and cost the team the most support time.

What changed.

  • Fewer people dropped off at payment once fees and the amount received were visible upfront.
  • "Where is my money?" questions became rarer once every transaction showed its progress.
  • Low-balance warnings caught empty accounts before ads stopped, instead of after.

What improving a live product taught me.

  • Data before opinions. Without clean tracking, every discussion was a guess. Fixing the data first made decisions faster and easier to agree on.
  • Small changes, measured. Shipping one flow at a time meant every result could be traced back to the change behind it.
  • Money needs clarity. When money is involved, uncertainty feels like risk. Showing cost and status upfront did more than any visual polish.

The question I started with

What stops partners and brands from trusting an affiliate platform enough to grow on it?

Context

Permate is an affiliate marketing platform in Vietnam. Brands publish offers, partners (KOCs, bloggers, YouTubers and deal sites) promote them with tracked links, and both sides need to agree on what each click and conversion was worth.

My role

The product was being built from scratch. As the UX researcher, I talked to the people who would use it, turned what I heard into insights, and worked with the BA and the product designer so those insights became features and user stories.

A plan before any pixels.

W1W2W3W4W5W6W7W8
Desk research & competitors
Interviews
Survey
Synthesis
Usability tests

Who I talked to.

Two sides of the same deal. I recruited both, because a platform that only one side trusts doesn't grow.

9 partners KOCs, bloggers and deal sites earning commission on sales
5 brands Affiliate managers at retail and finance brands

Illustrative numbers

Asking at scale.

Interviews told me why. A short survey told me how many. I sent one version to partners and one to brands, each under five minutes, so busy creators and affiliate managers would actually finish it.

Survey questions recreated for this case study

From notes to insights.

Every interview and open survey answer became a sticky note. I clustered them in rounds: first by what people said, then by why it mattered, until each cluster pointed to one insight the team could act on.

The partner journey.

Mapping the journey showed where confidence dropped. The low points weren't at the start, where we expected them, but after the work was done: tracking results and getting paid.

What we heard, what we built.

"I post a link and then I just hope it counts."Partner, paraphrased

Insight

Partners don't distrust the brand, they distrust what they can't see. Without a record of each click, every missing conversion feels like a lost commission.

What we built

A live activity log that shows every click and conversion, with the attribution status of each sale.

"I never know when I'll get paid, or why it's less than I expected."Partner, paraphrased

Insight

The money arrived eventually. The anxiety came from not knowing the rules: thresholds, approval windows and refunds.

What we built

A payout timeline from pending to approved to paid, with the threshold, the expected date and a reason for every adjustment.

"I approve partners blind. All I get is an email address."Brand, paraphrased

Insight

Brands wanted more partners, but couldn't tell good ones from risky ones, so applications piled up.

What we built

An application review screen showing each partner's channels, audience and track record, with bulk approve for the clear cases.

Testing before building.

I ran two rounds of usability tests on the product designer's prototype. Round one showed where people still got lost; we fixed those screens and tested again before development started.

Research in the room.

  • Weekly readoutsShort sessions with the BA and product designer, so findings landed while decisions were still open.
  • Insights linked to storiesEvery key user story pointed back to the insight behind it, so the team knew why it mattered.
  • One shared repositoryNotes, recordings and themes in one place, so anyone could check the evidence themselves.

What research changed.

  • The first release was built around tracking and payouts, not the marketplace features first planned.
  • Usability issues were found and fixed in the prototype, before any code was written.
  • Brands reviewed and approved applications in round two without asking for help.

What research on a 0→1 product taught me.

  • Talk to both sides. In a two-sided product, one side's pain is often caused by the other. Hearing both made the real problem visible.
  • Research is only useful if it lands. Insights mattered when they reached the BA and designer in time to change a decision.
  • Test the prototype, not the product. Fixing a screen in a prototype cost hours. Fixing it after release would have cost weeks.

How do you measure UX success?

A practical way to prove a design worked: decide what success means before you design, measure it at three levels, and always pair a number with the reason behind it.

Đỗ Hữu Thạnh8 min readNovember 2026

On this page Start with a question Three layers of evidence Give numbers a reference Every number needs a why Traps I try to avoid My checklist In my projects

For a long time I treated client approval as the finish line. If the stakeholder said yes in review, the design was done.

Ecomdy changed that. The top-up screens had passed every review, yet support tickets about top-ups kept coming every week. Approval told me people liked the screens. It did not tell me whether advertisers could add money before their ads stopped.

Since then I think of UX success as three questions. Can people do what they came for? Do they keep doing it? And does the business feel the difference?

The short version
  1. Decide what success means before designing: goal, then signal, then metric.
  2. Measure three layers: can they do it, do they do it, does it matter.
  3. Pair every number with a reason. Analytics show what happened, research shows why.
  4. Compare against a baseline or a benchmark, never against nothing.

Start with a question, not a dashboard.

Most teams open Google Analytics and look for something interesting. You get plenty of numbers that way, but very few answers.

Google's HEART framework, published by Kerry Rodden, Hilary Hutchinson and Xin Fu at CHI 2010, works the other way round. First you write the goal. Then you name the user behaviour that would show you reached it. Only then do you choose the number that tracks that behaviour. They call this Goals, Signals, Metrics.

HEART gives five kinds of goal to choose from. You don't need all five. Pick the two or three that match what this release is for.

A new feature lives or dies on adoption. An ERP screen that an accountant uses eight hours a day is about task success: fewer steps, fewer mistakes. Choosing the category is already half a design decision.

Three layers of evidence.

When I say a design worked, I want evidence at three levels. Each one answers a different question and arrives at a different time.

Usability numbers come fast and are clearly about the design. Business numbers are what leadership asks about, but many things move them at once: marketing, pricing, the season. So I report all three, and I say honestly how confident I am that the design caused the change.

Give every number a reference.

"Our SUS score is 72." Is that good? On its own, a number means nothing. I compare it with two things: our own baseline before the change, and published benchmarks.

The System Usability Scale (John Brooke, 1996) is ten short questions scored from 0 to 100. Across thousands of studies collected by MeasuringU, the average score is 68.

I use benchmarks as a sanity check, not a target. A tool that people use all day should beat the average by a wide margin. A first prototype that lands below it is simply telling you where to look next.

Every number needs a why.

Christian Rohrer at Nielsen Norman Group maps research methods on two axes: what people say versus what they do, and why versus how many. A good measurement plan takes something from more than one corner.

On Ecomdy, Google Analytics showed where the top-up flow lost people. Hotjar recordings showed why.

Without the recordings, the funnel would only have said "the confirm step is bad". Without the funnel, the recordings would have been a few stories with no sense of scale. Together they gave the team a clear change to make.

Traps I try to avoid.

  1. Measuring what is easy instead of what matters.

    Page views are easy to count. "Did they top up in time?" takes a tracking plan, but it is the number that answers the question.

  2. Turning the metric into the goal.

    Goodhart's law, in Marilyn Strathern's words: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Cut time on task by removing a confirmation step and errors go up. I pair every target with a guardrail metric that must not get worse.

  3. Reading time on task only one way.

    In a checkout, more time usually means confusion. On a page someone wants to read, it can mean interest. Decide which direction is good before you look.

  4. Trusting the average.

    An average rating of 4.2 can hide a group of users at 2.0. On Permate, partners and brands had very different pain points. Split results by role, device or plan before drawing conclusions.

  5. Proving things with five users.

    Five users are enough to find most of the big problems in a design (Nielsen). They are not enough to quote a success rate. For a number you can defend, you need a much larger sample, or real usage data.

My checklist.

Before designing
  • Write the goal, signal and metric
  • Record the baseline
  • Agree on one or two guardrail metrics
While designing
  • Test the prototype with 5–8 users on the key tasks
  • Note task success and ease for each task
  • Fix, then test again
After launch
  • Add tracking events before release, not after
  • Compare with the baseline at two and four weeks
  • Share a one-page readout: the number, the why, the next step

Where this shows up in my projects.

EcomdyFunnels and recordings to find where top-ups failedBehaviour · Business PermateTask success across two rounds of prototype testsUsability Student WorksFewer manual steps and errors in daily operationsUsability · Business

In the end, I count a design as successful when people stop noticing it, and the team can see the difference in a number it already cares about. Everything else is how you collect the evidence.

Sources

  1. Rodden, Hutchinson & Fu. Measuring the User Experience on a Large Scale: User-Centered Metrics for Web Applications. CHI 2010.
  2. Jeff Sauro. 10 Benchmarks for User Experience Metrics. MeasuringU.
  3. John Brooke. SUS: A "quick and dirty" usability scale. 1996.
  4. Christian Rohrer. When to Use Which User-Experience Research Methods. Nielsen Norman Group.
  5. Jakob Nielsen. Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users. Nielsen Norman Group.
  6. Marilyn Strathern. 'Improving ratings': audit in the British University system. 1997.

A UX hand-off checklist.

The list I run before marking a design ready for development. It catches the states, rules and edge cases a mockup quietly skips, so developers build the right thing the first time.

Đỗ Hữu Thạnh6 min readNovember 2026

On this page Why hand-off breaks The checklist Annotate the why A meeting, not a file What changed

Most bugs I saw after release were not on the main screen. They lived in the cases nobody drew.

In ERP and accounting products, those cases are everywhere: the empty list on day one, the closed accounting period, the user who can view but not approve, the invoice total with eleven digits. When the mockup doesn't show them, developers guess. Each guess becomes a bug ticket, a Slack thread or a quiet inconsistency.

So before I hand anything over, I go through one checklist. It is not a ceremony. It is the cheapest way I know to move problems from bug reports back into design review.

The short version
  1. Design every state, not just the happy path.
  2. Write business rules next to the screen they affect.
  3. Use real-length data and real formats.
  4. Hand off in a conversation with dev, QA and BA, then review the build.

Why hand-off breaks.

A mockup shows one moment: the screen with good data, a user with full access, everything loaded. A developer has to build every moment around it. The gap between those two is where most rework comes from.

Figma's own guide to developer hand-off makes the same point from the other side: bring developers in early, keep work in progress, ready-for-review and ready-to-build clearly separated, and connect every component back to its source. The checklist below is how I make that concrete.

The full list.

Six groups, ticked off before a design moves to "Ready for dev". Try it on your current file. Your ticks stay in this browser.

Annotate the why, not just the what.

Spacing and colours can be read straight from the file. What developers can't read is the rule behind a screen. That is what I annotate.

Rules written this way do double duty. QA turns them into test cases, and the BA can check them against the requirement without opening a design tool.

Hand-off is a meeting, not a file.

A link dropped in a ticket is not a hand-off. I treat it as a short series of conversations that starts long before the design is finished.

Since our team moved to AI-assisted prototypes, the package has grown. Next to the Figma file, I now hand over a clickable HTML prototype for complex flows and a structured list of screens, states and rules. Developers see the behaviour, not just a picture of it.

Figma file with a "Ready for dev" page Clickable prototype States and rules, annotated Tracking events Open questions log

What changed.

  • Fewer "what happens when…" questions.Most of them were already answered on the screen.
  • Edge cases moved earlier.They came up in design review instead of bug reports.
  • One list for everyone.QA wrote test cases from the same states and rules the developers built from.

A good hand-off feels a bit boring. Nobody is surprised, because every awkward case was already on the table. That is the point of the checklist.

Sources

  1. Figma. Guide to Developer Handoff: a collection of best practices from the experts.
  2. W3C. Understanding SC 2.5.8: Target Size (Minimum), WCAG 2.2.
  3. W3C. Understanding SC 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum), WCAG 2.2.

Thạnh

About me

I like problems that come with rules.

I'm Thạnh, a product designer in Vietnam working on ERP, accounting and e-commerce products. I enjoy the moment a messy process turns into a flow that makes sense. I keep learning new ways to work, and I usually raise my hand when something new comes up.

Logic first✦Always learning✦Ready for new challenges✦ Logic first✦Always learning✦Ready for new challenges✦
Drag to move

Who I am.

Logic

I like knowing why things work.

I'm the person who reads the rules before playing the game. Give me a messy process and I'll want to draw it out: where it loops, where it breaks, what it is really trying to do. Making sense of complicated things is what keeps me interested.

Learning

I'm curious by default.

I started in UX, then picked up business analysis, data and now AI tools, mostly because I wanted to see the whole picture, not just my part of it. When something new shows up, my first reaction is to try it, break it and figure out how it fits.

Challenge

I'd rather stretch than stay comfortable.

Some of the work I'm proudest of started with "I've never done this before". I'd rather be slightly out of my depth and learning fast than comfortable and standing still. New problems are the fun part.

Why product design.

Product design is where the three things I enjoy most meet: logic, people, and making something real.

I was never only interested in how a screen looks. I wanted to know how the business behind it works, why people get stuck, and which small change would make the biggest difference.

Product design lets me do all of that in one job. One day I'm untangling a business rule with a BA, the next I'm watching someone struggle with a form, and the day after I'm turning both into something a developer can build.

It never gets boring, because there is always another rule to understand and another person to design for.

What I believe.

01Ask why until the logic holds.

A request is usually a symptom. I keep asking until I find the rule or the pain behind it.

02Simple is earned.

The simplest screens often hide the most thinking. I'd rather do the hard work so people don't have to.
